name: Seasonal beauty care routines

card.summary: Adjusting skincare through the year, for example richer moisturisers in cold dry months and lighter textures with sunscreen in summer, to keep skin looking balanced.
card.note: Individual skin type and conditions determine what suits a person; dermatologists advise seeing one if dryness persists.

quick.overview:
Seasonal beauty care routines mean changing the products and steps in a skincare routine as the weather changes: heavier creams and gentler cleansing when air is cold and dry, lighter hydration and daily sun protection in warm months. The aim is skin that looks comfortable and even year round instead of flaky in winter or oily in summer.

The habit is associated with Korean beauty culture, which uses multi-step routines of cleansers, essences, serums, moisturisers and sunscreen.
quick.how: People keep a base routine and swap individual steps by season, such as a cream or ointment for a lotion in winter, or extra hydrating layers and more sunscreen in summer.
quick.risks: Switching too many products at once can irritate skin. The American Academy of Dermatology advises avoiding products with alcohol, fragrance or retinoids on very dry skin and seeing a dermatologist if dryness persists.

lead: Seasonal beauty care routines are the practice of adjusting skincare to the time of year. In Korean beauty culture, which commonly uses roughly ten-step regimens from double cleansing to sunscreen, routines are tailored to factors such as hormones and lifestyle.[1]

Dermatologists describe cold, low-humidity conditions as worsening dry skin and advise humidifiers, shorter warm showers, fragrance-free creams or ointments applied to damp skin, and protective clothing.[2]

chain: Match products to weather and humidity
Keep skin barrier hydrated and protected
angle.text: Skin appearance depends on hydration and protection, so swapping textures and sun care with the seasons targets dryness in winter and oil or sun exposure in summer.

paras: K-beauty regimens include double cleansing, sheet masks, essences, serums, rich moisturisers and SPF by day, with a thicker sleep cream at night.[1]

sections.h: Dermatologist guidance for cold, dry conditions
paras: The AAD advises a humidifier, 5 to 10 minute warm showers, moisturising several times a day, choosing creams or ointments over lotions, and protecting skin with gloves in cold weather.[2]
No studies found of seasonal routine switching as a practice. Dermatology guidance on dry-skin care is a broader category and is summarised above.
